tracks.title: One command, every verb
tracks.text: Last lesson — wbx. The command line. wbx is one compiled tool that authors, builds, signs, ships, and docks workbooks. The same binary on your laptop… in CI… and inside the engine. [curious] So you and your agents speak one language.

tracks.title: A bag of binaries
tracks.text: The problem — a bag of binaries. Every ecosystem eventually hands you a toolbelt. One binary to scaffold… another to build… a third to deploy… a wrapper to sign things… a daemon's client for the server bits. Each with its own flags, its own config file, its own way of being slightly out of date. [chuckles] You don't learn the tools, so much as negotiate with them. An ecosystem whose whole bet is homogeneity can't ship that. If workbooks are one artifact, and the grammar is one grammar… the tooling has to be one tool.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. wbx is the Workbooks command line. One compiled tool that authors, builds, signs, ships, and docks workbooks. The same binary on your laptop, in CI, and inside the engine. And it's deliberately thin. wbx owns almost no logic of its own. It parses what you asked… handles local org operations with the same kernel the rest of the ecosystem uses… and drives the engine for everything heavy. The intelligence lives in the system. wbx is the handle.

tracks.title: Install it
tracks.text: Installing is one line. Curl workbooks dot s h, slash c l i dot s h… piped to shell. It detects your OS and architecture. Or npm install — same thing, npm-flavored. macOS, Linux, and Windows binaries all ship from the releases. Then, let the tool check itself. Two commands. First — wbx doctor. It reports your environment and engine health… what's wired, and what isn't. And second — bare wbx, no arguments. A where-am-I landing. Version… engine state… and your likely next moves.

tracks.title: The verb families
tracks.text: Thirty-odd verbs. But they group into families — and if you learn the families, the help text carries you the rest of the way. Six of them. First: author. Init, dev, query, lint… org in, structure out. Second: make. Build and bundle — compile code to WebAssembly, tangle everything into one artifact. Third: trust. Sign and verify… provenance that travels with the file. Fourth: parts. The toolkit family — discover, build, push, import, run. Fifth: engine. Deploy, publish, workbook… stand up a Nexus, and ship to it. And sixth: the everyday verbs. Doctor… status… open… upgrade. Plus the library verbs, off to the side — store, fetch, search, check out, and check in. Every family follows the same manners. [excited] And every success suggests the next verb. The tool teaches its own grammar as you go.

tracks.title: Two audiences, one binary
tracks.text: Two audiences… one binary. Here's the design decision that shapes everything else. wbx knows it has two kinds of users… and it changes its manners for each — without changing what it does. You, at a terminal? Human mode is deliberately dumb simple. The tool does the work. Missing argument with an obvious default? It picks the default… and tells you. Every success ends with the next verb you probably want. An agent, in a pipe? The moment stdout isn't a terminal, wbx switches. No prompts… ever. No color codes. Plain, parseable output. Add the JSON flag, and every outcome — success or failure — arrives as one envelope. A stable error code… a message… and a hint written for the agent to act on. [excited] Failures carry a stable exit-code map, so a script can branch without parsing prose. Three means the engine's unreachable — and it's retryable. Four means not found. Seven means your credentials got rejected. [chuckles] Don't retry that one blindly.

tracks.title: Your first workbook, two minutes
tracks.text: Your first workbook — two minutes, nothing assumed. You need wbx installed… that's it. No engine. No account. Step one: scaffold. wbx init, field notes. One command… one folder. Step two: see it live. wbx dev watches the org file, re-renders on every save, and serves a preview that reloads itself. Open the URL… open the org file in any editor… change a heading… save. [excited] And watch the browser follow. That loop — org file on the left, living page on the right — is the whole authoring experience. And step three: make it one carton. wbx bundle packs the workbook html, the source, and the data into a single self-contained bundle — field notes dot wbundle. Then wbx sign puts your name on it… provenance embedded in the artifact. The carton ships anywhere. The workbook html riding inside opens in any browser… and mails like an attachment. No server was involved at any point.

tracks.title: Import anything
tracks.text: Import anything. You probably already have capability lying around… and the intake ramp packages any of it as a toolkit. Nine source kinds detect by shape. First: Claude skills — docs become org, scripts come along. Second: MCP servers — a skill per server… secrets never enter the artifact, env vars carry over by name only. Third: OpenAPI specs — a skill per operation. Fourth: npm and pip CLIs — the readme becomes the manual. And fifth: plain guidance docs… a perfectly valid landing. Point wbx toolkit import at the thing — the reply reads: imported… manifest written… audited two scripts — one ready, one convertible, zero blocked. That audit is stage two of three. Stage one parses and scaffolds. Stage two classifies every script against the sandbox lanes — ready… convertible… or blocked — and the findings land in the manifest, so the artifact carries its own audit. And stage three writes the fix-up plan. Everything not ready becomes a to-do — a blocked python script's entry reads: rewrite in JS for the quickjs lane… then re-run the audit. [excited] Hand the folder to an agent — the work is already itemized. And when an engine is reachable… audit, dash dash fix. One shot.

tracks.title: Wire in an agent
tracks.text: Pointing a coding agent at wbx? Three things make it fluent immediately. First — let it discover the surface. wbx help, dash dash JSON, returns the entire verb tree as machine-readable structure. An agent never guesses at flags. Second — give it the envelope. Call everything with the JSON flag… branch on the error code and the retryable bit… instead of scraping stderr. The hint field literally names the command that fixes the problem. And third — pipe freely. Author verbs accept dash, for standard input… so generated org never needs a temp file. That's the whole integration. No SDK. No API keys for the local surface. The same binary you use… spoken plainly.

tracks.title: Same binary everywhere
tracks.text: Same binary, everywhere — the part that makes wbx more than a convenience. It's one Rust crate… with two build targets. The native binary is what you install. The same source also compiles to WebAssembly — so it runs inside the engine's sandbox. Which means the agents working in a runtime container reach for the exact same tool you do. Same help text. Same manners. That's not an implementation detail… it's the trust model. When an agent's session log says wbx toolkit build, you can run the identical command and see the identical thing. So watch one real session, start to finish — one tool, the whole journey. wbx init — a folder appears. wbx dev — a living preview that follows every save. wbx bundle — out comes field notes dot wbundle… shippable, source riding inside. wbx sign — provenance embedded. wbx deploy local — a runtime comes up on your machine. wbx workbook deploy — docked… living at slash w slash notes. wbx toolkit import on a Claude skill… then wbx toolkit push. [excited] And your skill is on the agents' path now. One tool the whole way — and your agents are holding the same one.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need the engine installed? Not for the local families. Author, make, and trust work on plain files. Windows? Yes — as of oh-thirteen, it ships in every release. What's the difference between agent mode and the JSON flag? Agent mode is manners — no prompts, no color. JSON is a format — the envelope contract. Most integrations want both… [chuckles] piping gets you the first for free. And — can it really convert my Claude skill into a toolkit? It packages anything parseable, immediately. Scripts are the honest part. Shell and JavaScript usually classify ready… python is blocked until there's a lane… and everything in between gets a written fix-up plan. Rather than a shrug.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: And that's wbx. One command… every verb… the same binary in every hand that holds it. That's the whole tour. The file… the engine… the parts… the grammar… the agents… the gardener… and the command. [excited] Now go make something — and hand it to someone.
